## Summary

Research confidence is **Moderate**. Some of this break's ideal conditions are confirmed by sources; others rest on limited evidence. It is the class the app computes from the evidence (how well the break's ideal conditions are documented), not a forecast and not a probability.

Main gaps:

- Limited information is available about this break's preferred tide conditions.
- Limited information is available about the swell period this break needs.
- Only one independent source confirms the best wind direction.
- No survey, scientific or official source confirms the wave size this break works in.

| Variable | Research confidence | Evidence |

| Swell direction | High | Supported by 5 independent sources, including a forecast site's spot guide. |
| Swell size | Moderate | Supported by 3 independent sources, including a surf magazine. |
| Swell period | Low | Supported by one source (a surf magazine) (based on search summaries; source pages not read in full) |
| Wind | Moderate | Supported by one source (a forecast site's spot guide). |
| Tide | Low | No sources found. |

| How the wave breaks | High | Described by 5 independent sources, including a published surf guide. |

Research notes (research_evidence.json):

> Re-read 6 of 8 current sources. surfertoday.com returned 403 and visitmexico.com gave no response (status 0), so both are kept unchanged as web_search. Visit Mexico's source_type was changed to magazine, because tourism boards are not official under v1.2, and WSL pages are now magazine too. New readable sources: The Inertia (2018) and Surf Atlas (2025). Wind remains the weak variable. Only surf-forecast.com gives a direction: NE (45), matching the profile's 40, after correcting the earlier NNE. The Inertia, WannaSurf and Surf Atlas agree mornings are offshore until about 10-11 am, but give no direction. WannaSurf's 'Good wind direction: SouthWest' would be onshore at this south-facing beach and looks like a data error. Direction is strongly supported: WSL 180-225, surf-forecast SSW, WannaSurf SW, Surf Atlas S. WSL's 163-280 window is close to the profile's 150-260; the WSL piece was written with Surfline forecasters' help. Size: WannaSurf gives 3-5 ft to 16 ft+ and WSL a 20-25 ft contest day. The Inertia says it handles 30 ft peaks, above the profile's 25 ft maximum. Wikipedia's 'up to sixteen metres' is a record figure and was not recorded. Tide: still no source (the profile says mid). Period: no readable number. WSL's '15 seconds apart... 25 seconds apart' is general swell physics, not a Puerto preference, so it was not recorded. Bathymetry conflict: most sources describe sandbars over an offshore canyon/trench (WSL, Stormrider, The Inertia), while WannaSurf lists reef with sand. Season: all readable sources fall within April-October, inside or near the profile's April-September.

## Ideal conditions

Directions are compass degrees the swell or wind comes FROM, ranges clockwise. Heights keep the scale each source states (breaking face, Hawaiian, swell or relative to the surfer); the app's sizes are breaking face heights in feet. Sources are numbered as in [Sources](#sources).

### Swell height

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum suitable | 3–5 ft | documented | S3, S7 | `wave_height_min_ft` 4 ft (breaking face) |
| Ideal range | — | not documented | — | no separate setting; working range 4–25 ft |
| Maximum suitable | 30 ft [S7] · 19 ft [S10] · 16 ft and over (open-ended) [S3] | conflicting | S3, S7, S10 | `wave_height_max_ft` 25 ft (breaking face) |

Notes:

- **Minimum suitable**: WannaSurf says it starts working at 1.0-1.5 m / 3-5 ft (scale not stated) and The Inertia says it handles anything from chest-high waves (a face height relative to the surfer).
  - S3 (WannaSurf): “Swell sizeStarts working at 1.0m-1.5m / 3ft-5ft and holds up to 5m / 16 ft and over”
  - S7 (The Inertia): “which can handle anything from chest-high waves to the monstrous barrels...The ability for a beach break to handle 30ft peaks is owed to the submarine trench lying offshore.”
- **Ideal range**: No excerpt gives an ideal size.
- **Maximum suitable**: The Inertia says the beach break can handle 30 ft peaks, Visit Mexico (search summary) describes waves up to 19 ft, and WannaSurf's top bracket (5 m / 16 ft and over) is open-ended; none states the scale.
  - S7 (The Inertia): “which can handle anything from chest-high waves to the monstrous barrels...The ability for a beach break to handle 30ft peaks is owed to the submarine trench lying offshore.”
  - S10 (Visit Mexico (official tourism portal)): “Zicatela is described as having waves up to 19 feet high.”
  - S3 (WannaSurf): “Swell sizeStarts working at 1.0m-1.5m / 3ft-5ft and holds up to 5m / 16 ft and over”

### Swell direction

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ideal bearing | 180–225° (S to SW, clockwise) | documented | S2, S3, S4, S8, S9 | `optimal_swell_direction` 190–225° (S to SW, clockwise) |
| Acceptable range | 163–280° (SSE to W, clockwise) | documented | S4 | `swell_window` 150–260° (SSE to W, clockwise) |
| Blocked directions | — | not documented | — | no separate setting (outside `swell_window`) |
| Exposure | exposed; open to the Pacific from 163 to 280 deg | documented | S2, S4 | no setting |

Notes:

- **Ideal bearing**: WSL says big swells between 180 and 225 deg make it pump, Surf-Forecast gives SSW, WannaSurf SW, the Surf Atlas southerlies from the Southern Ocean, and SurferToday (search summary) SW groundswells plus westerly hurricane swells.
  - S4 (World Surf League): “it's the big swells between 225 degrees and 180 degrees that make Puerto pump into the XXL category”
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “the best swell direction is from the south southwest”
  - S3 (WannaSurf): “Good swell directionSouthWest”
  - S8 (Surf Atlas): “May to August feels the full brunt of southerlies from the Southern Ocean.”
  - S9 (SurferToday): “Zicatela starts working with southwest groundswells, and westerly hurricane swells.”
- **Acceptable range**: WSL says it is open to everything in the Pacific from 280 deg (west) to 163 deg (south-southeast).
  - S4 (World Surf League): “It's open to everything happening in the Pacific from 280 degrees west to 163 degrees south-southeast.”
- **Blocked directions**: No excerpt names blocked directions (the Surf Atlas claim text mentions missed N-NW winter swells, but its excerpt does not).
- **Exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it an exposed beach break and WSL gives its open window as 163-280 deg.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “an exposed beach break that has pretty consitent surf...The beach break provides left and right handers.”
  - S4 (World Surf League): “It's open to everything happening in the Pacific from 280 degrees west to 163 degrees south-southeast.”

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prime months | common to all sources: Jul, Aug; widest stated: Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Oct | documented | S1, S2, S3, S6, S8, S9 | `best_months` Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep |

Notes:

- **Prime months**: Stormrider and SurferToday (search summary) give April-October, the Surf Atlas May-September, Surf-Forecast and WannaSurf the (northern) summer and Wikipedia mid to late summer, so July-August is common to every reading and April-October is the widest stated.
  - S6 (Stormrider Surf Guides): “the swell from both the Southern Hemisphere and frequent tropical storms that pass by this coast in summer time (April-Oct)”
  - S9 (SurferToday): “One guide lists the season as April-October.”
  - S8 (Surf Atlas): “The summer between May and September is the peak time to surf in Puerto Escondido and will be when Zicatela is firing to its full potential.”
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Summer offers the favoured conditions for surfing.”
  - S3 (WannaSurf): “The waves are at its biggest in the summer when most other summers are small.”
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “Mid to late summer is low season for tourists, but a prime time for waves and international tournaments.”
- **Secondary season**: No excerpt describes a secondary season.
- **Swell sources**: Stormrider names Southern Hemisphere swell and frequent tropical storms, the Surf Atlas Southern Ocean southerlies, and SurferToday (search summary) SW groundswells and westerly hurricane swells.
  - S6 (Stormrider Surf Guides): “the swell from both the Southern Hemisphere and frequent tropical storms that pass by this coast in summer time (April-Oct)”
  - S8 (Surf Atlas): “May to August feels the full brunt of southerlies from the Southern Ocean.”
  - S9 (SurferToday): “Zicatela starts working with southwest groundswells, and westerly hurricane swells.”
- **Wind patterns**: The Inertia and WannaSurf describe morning offshores, an onshore wind from about 10-11 am and offshore again later, the Surf Atlas says midday can bring cross-shores, and SurferToday (search summary) says early morning is best while the offshore blows.
  - S7 (The Inertia): “It will be offshore every morning from first light until about 11 am, blowing onshore for part of the day before turning offshore again late afternoon.”
  - S3 (WannaSurf): “Surf early in the morning to avoid the typical onshore wind which gets up from around 10-11h but which turns offshore again before the night.”
  - S8 (Surf Atlas): “Mornings are the best, with heavy sets pounding onto the beachfront. However, midday can get blazing hot and even catch some cross shores that mess it up a little.”
  - S9 (SurferToday): “Early morning is usually best, when the offshore winds are blowing and there are fewer people in the water.”

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Break type | beach (sandbars of Playa Zicatela) | documented | S2, S5 | `break_type` beach, `wave_direction` both |

| Exposure | exposed | documented | S2 | no setting |
| Bathymetry | sandbars in front of offshore submarine canyons / a deep-water trench with no continental shelf [S4, S5, S6, S7] · reef (coral, sharp rocks) with sand [S3] | conflicting | S3, S4, S5, S6, S7 | no measured bathymetry (profile derived from the swell windows) |

Notes:

- **Break type**: Surf-Forecast calls it an exposed beach break with lefts and rights, and WSL describes waves pounding the sandbars of Playa Zicatela.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “an exposed beach break that has pretty consitent surf...The beach break provides left and right handers.”
  - S5 (World Surf League): “pounding the sandbars of Playa Zicatela”
- **Orientation**: No excerpt gives the beach orientation.
- **Exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it an exposed beach break.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “an exposed beach break that has pretty consitent surf...The beach break provides left and right handers.”
- **Bathymetry**: WSL, Stormrider and The Inertia describe sandbars in front of offshore submarine canyons or a deep-water trench that focuses the swell, whereas WannaSurf lists a reef bottom with sand.
  - S4 (World Surf League): “just off the coast of this stretch of beach are a series of underwater submarine canyons. One of the canyons has a finger that points directly to the northern half of the beach.”
  - S5 (World Surf League): “pounding the sandbars of Playa Zicatela”
  - S6 (Stormrider Surf Guides): “The lack of any continental shelf and the offshore deep-water trench focuses the swell...These swells hit the sandbars in such a way that the waves jack-up in size”
  - S7 (The Inertia): “Here, big swells pour in and hit the steep shelf quickly, jacking up and producing the waves that make the place famous.”
  - S7 (The Inertia): “which can handle anything from chest-high waves to the monstrous barrels...The ability for a beach break to handle 30ft peaks is owed to the submarine trench lying offshore.”
  - S3 (WannaSurf): “BottomReef (coral,sharp rocks etc..) with sand”

## Conflicting information

- **Swell height · maximum suitable**: The Inertia says the beach break can handle 30 ft peaks, Visit Mexico (search summary) describes waves up to 19 ft, and WannaSurf's top bracket (5 m / 16 ft and over) is open-ended; none states the scale.
- **Geography · bathymetry**: WSL, Stormrider and The Inertia describe sandbars in front of offshore submarine canyons or a deep-water trench that focuses the swell, whereas WannaSurf lists a reef bottom with sand.
